g.text: At launch, on returning to the foreground, after login and before sign-up.
Each check asks one question: is this device or its Apple Account banned?
idfv, an installId kept in the Keychain and, with useICloud, the iCloud user ID; after login, your user ID too.
Only SHA-256 hashes leave the iPhone, never the raw values.
It asks DeviceCheck for two one-time tokens
One token lets the Worker query the device’s bits at Apple, the other lets it update them.
Apple asks for each token to be used only once, so there is one for each job.
It sends the hashes and tokens to your Worker
A Cloudflare Worker that you deploy yourself, one per app.
The Worker makes the decision; your app’s own backend isn’t involved.
The Worker checks its ban list in D1
Is any of these hashes banned?
D1 stores hashes only: no raw identifiers and no IP addresses.
bit0 means banned. It lives on Apple’s servers, so it is still there after the iPhone is erased.
If the list bans the device and bit0 isn’t set yet, the Worker sets it.
blocked comes with a support code (ref), and your app shows its suspended screen.
If the check fails and the device has no earlier block, the user gets in (fail-open).
A blocked device spreads the ban
The Worker adds the device’s new hashes to the list, so the ban can follow its Apple Account to other iPhones.
In observation mode (ENFORCE off) it only records what it would block, and answers ok.
Four layers make the ban stick
Each layer survives a different way of starting over, so together they cover each other’s gaps.
Only hashes leave the iPhone. Your Worker decides with its D1 list and Apple’s bit0,
and each layer survives a different way of starting over.
records new hashes if it blocks.
Hashes only. No raw values, no IPs.
Four layers, each survives something different
